analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $10.10 an hour over two years and indexes it to inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage to $10.10 an hour was referred to a Senate committee on March 5, 2013 and never received another action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour to $8.20, then $9.15, then $10.10 over about two years, and then adjusted it automatically each year with inflation so it would never again lose value while waiting for Congress to act. It also raised the separate minimum wage for tipped workers to $3.00 and put it on a path to reach 70% of the full minimum wage. The bill was sent to the Senate committee that handles labor issues on the day it was introduced and never moved again; it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage would have received raises of up to $2.85 an hour — a roughly 39% increase from $7.25 to $10.10 — plus automatic inflation adjustments thereafter. Tipped workers, whose cash minimum had been frozen at $2.13 since 1991, would have seen their base wage rise toward 70% of the full minimum.

how_it_helps.text: Raised the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $8.20, then $9.15, then $10.10 over roughly two years.
Tied the minimum wage to the Consumer Price Index after two years, so it would rise automatically with inflation instead of losing value until Congress acts again.
Raised the separate, much lower minimum wage for tipped employees and set it on a path to reach 70% of the full minimum wage.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum wages — restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service businesses — would have borne the higher labor costs, potentially passing some along as slightly higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Critics of minimum wage increases argue that raising the required wage raises labor costs for restaurants, retail, and other low-margin employers, which can lead to higher prices for consumers or fewer entry-level job opportunities for the least experienced workers.

The bill raised the tipped minimum more slowly than the general wage (reaching 70% of the full minimum over several years), so even after passage tipped workers would still have earned a base wage well below the standard minimum and remained dependent on tips to reach it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side was large and concrete: roughly three million-plus low-wage workers would have gotten a raise phased in to $10.10, with the indexation ensuring it never eroded again — the first time the federal minimum would have kept pace with prices automatically. The costs are real but modest by the best evidence: modest price pass-through in labor-intensive sectors and possible small reductions in new hiring among the least-experienced workers. On balance the gains to low-wage households outweighed those costs; the bill died anyway, so the question remained academic for this Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and it sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no further action for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2013 on March 5, 2013, joined by 25 original Senate cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the standard first step for a wage bill.
No further action appears in the record: the bill was never voted out of committee, never debated on the Senate floor, and never received a vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

The bill carried 33 cosponsors, all Democrats or the chamber's independent members, meaning it lacked the 60 votes typically needed to overcome a filibuster in the Senate even if it had reached the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the federal minimum wage kept the $7.25 floor and avoided the higher labor costs the bill would have imposed; low-wage workers got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers paying $7.25; the raise never happened

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-IA), bill sponsor and chairman of the Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks, but never brought it to a committee vote or the Senate floor before his committee.

for.name: 33 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed raising the federal minimum wage; as a bloc they would have furnished the votes to block any floor vote, though no individual action on this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independent; no Senate Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a recorded vote.

industries.note: Labor-intensive and heavy users of the tipped minimum wage, these employers would have faced the largest direct payroll increase, from the general wage floor to $10.10 and a higher base wage for tipped staff.
Businesses relying on minimum-wage labor would have seen higher wage costs, potentially passed to consumers as modestly higher prices.
Workers earning at or near the minimum wage would have seen direct pay raises, including the roughly one-third who are 40 or older, not just teenagers.
